functional.people: The designer who publishes a game; the GM at doors-open; a second designer later
functional.moment: Between games when the designer publishes, and at doors-open when agreement must be visible
functional.need: The whole kit plays that game, that version, with no code change: the engine scores by it, the TV shows its words, every tablet and scanner holds the same copy, and the GM can see at a glance that they match or is refused.
functional.proposedTitle: The designer's game is the game the whole kit plays

functional.people: The GM on any tablet; the audience reading the TV; in future games, a player with a hidden fact
functional.moment: Mid-show, at once, and after a tablet comes back
functional.need: Whatever the GM did on any tablet is what every tablet, the TV and the audience see: a delete frees the token everywhere, a reset empties every screen, and nobody has to ask which screen is right.
functional.proposedTitle: One game, the same on every screen

functional.people: The GM at a token or a button and the player at a token; the owner and the designer after the show
functional.moment: During play at every tap, and at the Review stage after the end
functional.need: At a tap on a token or a button they learn at once whether it counted and why not if it did not; nothing is silently lost or doubled. Afterwards the night's story is read from what was captured during play, not reconstructed.
functional.proposedTitle: Every tap gets its answer, and the night can be told afterwards

functional.people: The audience who see and hear the show; the GM at the Environment and Show Control sections
functional.moment: When the game says so, and whenever the GM presses a control
functional.need: The room does what the designer cued and what the GM asked; the GM sees it happen, or sees at once that it did not and what to press; a dead program comes back by itself before anyone notices.
functional.proposedTitle: The room does what the designer cued and the GM asked

functional.people: The GM who starts, pauses, ends and resets games; the designer whose edit lands between games
functional.moment: At each lifecycle button, at an engine restart, and when a pack changes
functional.need: Each act does exactly what its name says: an ended game stays ended, the next game starts clean, a restart during a show loses nothing, a pause blocks scans, and a between-games edit never reaches the game in progress.
functional.proposedTitle: Each lifecycle button does exactly what its name says

functional.people: The game designer; the owner designing the second game; a new designer learning from the toy game
functional.moment: In the days before a show, on a laptop or on the show machine between games
functional.need: Build a game or change one value in it, publish and apply it, and play a round within minutes, with nothing they do able to reach the live show or its records.
functional.proposedTitle: The designer changes a value and plays it within minutes, and the live show never notices

functional.people: The GM; the audience; a player with no account; a stranger on the venue wifi
functional.moment: At every connection and every command
functional.need: The GM alone can start, pause, end and change scores, and the engine knows which tablet did it; the audience sees scores and exposed evidence and nothing else; a player sees the memory they scanned; designers and venue technicians reach their tools and only those; a stranger sees nothing.
functional.proposedTitle: Each person sees their part and can do only their part

functional.people: The venue technician; a GM running a game with no engine; a future operator with a second kit
functional.moment: In the days before an event, and on the night when the engine is absent by choice
functional.need: The venue technician states what the kit brings tonight, binds the pack's names to real instruments and gets one go or no-go. A standalone game knows it is standalone instead of mourning a lost connection. A second kit needs no change to engine code.
functional.proposedTitle: The game fits the venue it is in tonight

functional.people: The GM mid-show with seconds to decide; the venue technician reading the preflight; the audience watching the clock
functional.moment: At a glance, whenever a screen is read
functional.need: Anyone can tell without asking whether what they see is current and whether they must act: red means act now, grey means absent on purpose, old looks old, the venue technician's go is a go, and the TV's clock never counts on its own.
functional.proposedTitle: Anyone reading a screen can act on it without a second question

functional.people: The developer who changes the engine; the owner who sends a version to the venue; the GM whose live show no test may touch
functional.moment: Before every change reaches anyone, and on release day
functional.need: A green run means the show path still works for ALN and for the toy game; the owner decides when a new version goes to the venue and can swap back by replugging a machine; no test or rehearsal ever reaches a live show.
functional.proposedTitle: A change is proven before it reaches anyone, and the owner alone sends it to the show

mechanisms.name: The rules
mechanisms.plain: What a mode means, what a token scores, when a group completes, whether a claim uses the token up, how money is written. Well built in the engine today, in one place that only calculates; hand-copied on the tablet, and read a third time by the TV from its own fetch.

mechanisms.name: Getting a fact onto a screen
mechanisms.plain: One route per fact, the same for the live change and the catch-up after a reconnect, carrying the fact's label. Today two builders per fact, four different ways the tablet writes a fact, the TV's own rules, and health on a different route from state.

mechanisms.name: Knowing who is connected
mechanisms.plain: A verified pass on every connection, the device's class and name, whether it is still there. Today spread over six engine modules; a hardware scanner is filed as a phone; only a connection that calls itself a GM is asked for a pass; five clients each show their own word for whether the engine is there. It also says who may move the game and command the room, and gives the design tool and a preview engine their own passes.

mechanisms.name: The boundary table
mechanisms.plain: At setup, start, pause, end, reset, restart, the next game and a pack change: what each fact and each copy keeps, clears or carries. Today boot and Reset System are two hand-kept lists, the tablet and the TV guess a boundary from a changed id, and player devices never learn one.

mechanisms.name: Reading and keeping alive an outside program
mechanisms.plain: One adapter per program, one supervision rule, the engine's picture of each program dated. Today seven adapters with no shared interface above them, two supervision shapes, and a private connected flag beside the shared health list.

mechanisms.name: The verdict
mechanisms.plain: What the game needs against what the kit has tonight, one calculation, each line paper or live, three health words. Built and in good shape today; its result reaches no screen except a session stamp and the text of an acknowledgement.

mechanisms.name: Answering a request
mechanisms.plain: A reply that says which request it answers, whether it is final, and whether anything was stored. Today three reply shapes at three doors, the tablet matching a reply to its request by the command's name alone, and the phone and the hardware scanner reading one status differently.

mechanisms.name: Keeping engines apart
mechanisms.plain: Every name an engine owns, its process files, sockets, ports, data folder, passes and the display it drives, is per engine. Today nothing: sixteen fixed temporary names, two machine-wide kills, and tests that adopt the live display and audio.

mechanisms.name: Publishing the pack to every holder
mechanisms.plain: One list of every copy, one way to fetch it, one notice that it changed, every copy showing which version it holds. Today nine holders, no message, and a publish that tells the running engine nothing.

mechanisms.name: Checking the joins
mechanisms.plain: Every name and shape two parts share is checked against both, test stand-ins against the real code, the same suite on two packs. Today three contract tests and the schema tests; the hardware scanner's file shape, the stand-ins, the scoreboard's reading of the snapshot and the media folders are not joined.

mechanisms.name: The authority switch
mechanisms.plain: Who decides each fact when there is no engine, and the declared fact that says a game is standalone. Not a part but a setting every rule must take into account. Today a tap on the tablet, a URL path on the phone, nothing on the hardware scanner, no field in the pack.

qualities.name: Honesty
qualities.plain: A screen never shows a calm normal value where the truth is unknown, old, broken or not installed tonight. Carried as a label on every delivered fact and every reply, with the three health words from the verdict.

qualities.name: Proof
qualities.plain: A passing test run means the show works for two games, and no test reaches a live show. Carried by testing each part through the same door everything else uses, and by giving every test run its own engine names.

qualities.name: Generic
qualities.plain: Nothing in the engine assumes ALN, one kit, one pack or one production. Carried by taking rules only from the pack and kit names only from the profile and the engine's own instance.

qualities.name: Who decides when there is no engine
qualities.plain: Every rule says who decides when there is no engine, and a standalone game is a declared fact, never mixed. Carried by hosting the same record, lifecycle and answering modules on the tablet, with the declaration held wherever the owner places it; the venue technician's profile is the candidate favoured here.

qualities.name: Only the GM moves the game
qualities.plain: Lifecycle, show control and score changes stay in the GM's hands. Carried by checking once, at the one door every request passes, what each connection may do.

tangles.title: The pack is held in nine places and nothing joins them
tangles.plain: The engine's frozen snapshot and the live disk bytes under it, the tablet's cache, the phone's own file, the hardware scanner's card, the TV's own fetch, the design tool's working copy, the sync script's output, two nested copies and media in three folders. No message says the pack changed, so after a publish the TV, the engine and a tablet can run three versions of one game.

tangles.title: The game's facts are decided once and re-decided in five parts
tangles.plain: The tablet marks a token claimed, computes the points and shows complete before the engine answers; the phone and the hardware scanner decide whether a token exists; the TV decides which modes count as evidence; a standalone tablet decides everything from a hand-kept copy of the rules. Eighteen rules are re-decided on clients, and for five of them nothing keeps the copies equal.

tangles.title: One fact, two builders; state and health on two routes
tangles.plain: For seven facts the snapshot a tablet gets on connect and the live message for the same fact are built by different code. A service's state and its health arrive as separate pushes. No fact carries an age, and no screen reads the ages that exist.

tangles.title: Three doors, three reply shapes, acknowledgements matched by name
tangles.plain: A player scan, a GM scan and a GM command each get a differently shaped reply. The tablet matches an acknowledgement to a request by the action name alone, so two quick presses cannot be told apart. The phone and the hardware scanner read the same status differently.

tangles.title: Who is connected has no home
tangles.plain: The engine asks a pass only of a connection that calls itself a GM; the TV calls itself a GM; the whole game state can be fetched with no pass; a health check registers a device and files a hardware scanner as a phone; the design tool runs a second login against the same password; five clients each draw their own reachability word.

tangles.title: The life of a game is carried in six places and owned by none
tangles.plain: Boot and Reset System are two hand-kept lists that differ; nineteen parts each reset themselves and Reset System calls fourteen of them; the record calls into the show from five places and the show calls back, a seven-module loop; the tablet and the TV guess a boundary from a changed id; the player devices' queues outlive every game; the engine undoes its own wiring only under test.

tangles.title: Equipment: seven adapters, no shared interface, a cached picture with no age
tangles.plain: Each program is read by parsing its text or its event stream. Whether a video is playing has several answerers; held cues and held videos live in two stores; the music player keeps a private connected flag beside the shared health list; supervision has two shapes.

tangles.title: The engine assumes it owns the machine, and tests assume they may use it
tangles.plain: Sixteen fixed temporary names, two machine-wide kills, media folders in fixed places and kit names in at least twelve files. Tests adopt the live display, audio and Bluetooth and write placeholder videos into the live media folder.

tangles.title: The tablet is a command center and a second engine in one, and the standalone choice is not a seam
tangles.plain: Four files carry a second copy of the rules; thirty of the tablet's sixty-seven files would carry a standalone game; the one strategy seam covers storage only, and twenty branches in six modules ask the mode directly; the four domain objects reach everything through a back-reference; three layer inversions make dependencies run both ways.

tangles.title: The design tool reaches the engine by file and by import, never by message
tangles.plain: It writes the engine's settings, routing file and media folders; imports engine modules by path; runs the engine's pack check as a child process. An edit becomes visible at the engine's next restart. There is no apply step, no preview engine and no statement of where one would run.

tangles.title: Joins kept by hand, fakes unchecked, tests per part
tangles.plain: Twelve test configurations by part and three contract tests that pin joins. Nothing checks the hardware scanner's token-file shape against the pack, a fake against its class or the scoreboard's reading of the snapshot. The deployed game is several checkouts, a built folder and hand-copied media that nothing compares.

tangles.title: Shallow chains and thick doors
tangles.plain: Skip video crosses five tablet modules to reach one deep one; one command dispatcher serves six promises; the player scan route decides token existence, session existence and video eligibility inline and holds a batch cache lost at restart; the engine's wiring is written by hand at about ten sites, and one of them already left music out.

tangles.title: The scoreboard page is one file, two deployments, and sits on both sides of the engine
tangles.plain: Nearly two thousand lines with no module boundary; it decides the evidence rule and the money format from a file it fetched; it extrapolates the countdown and keeps counting after a disconnect; the engine launches, shows, hides and kills its browser as an outside program while the page is a client of the engine under a pass minted into the page text.

parts.name: Game rules
parts.plain: The pack's rules as one body of code that the engine and a standalone tablet both run, which only calculates and changes nothing: what a mode means, what a token scores, when a group completes, whether a claim uses the token up, which phases allow a scan, how money is written. The hardware scanner gets the rules it needs as generated data tables.
parts.seams: One body of code run in two places, the engine and a standalone tablet; data tables for the hardware scanner. It reads and writes nothing and keeps no state.

parts.name: Pack channel
parts.plain: One list of every holder of the pack, one way to fetch it, one notice that it changed, and a version stamp every copy shows and every game record carries. Each media file is checked against the pack's list by a fingerprint of its content.
parts.seams: The pack source (a folder, the draft store, the toy packs). Adopt is called once per boundary by the lifecycle.

parts.name: Game record
parts.plain: The one place the game's facts are decided: teams, claims, scores, exposed evidence, player scans, the phase. It takes an action in and gives back the facts that changed, each dated. Claims are read from the transactions, never kept beside them.
parts.seams: Persistence (file or memory); the host (the engine in a networked game, the tablet in a standalone one, depending on whether the game is standalone).

parts.name: Answering
parts.plain: Every request, from a tap or a button, over any transport, gets one reply in one shape: which request it answers, the outcome word, whether it is final, whether anything was stored. The rule that only the GM may start, pause, end or change scores is checked here, once.
parts.seams: Web requests and the live connection both plug into one door; the player scanners read every reply from the same list of words.

parts.name: The night's record
parts.plain: When a game ends, one structured record of the night is written from the facts the engine decided, with the roster, notes, accusation and later photos captured into it during play. The owner and the designer read the night from it.
parts.seams: The written shape of the record, the session bundle; the designer's Review reads it.

parts.name: Delivery
parts.plain: One route per fact from where it is decided to every screen that may see it, the same route for the live change and for the catch-up after a reconnect, every fact carrying its label (what it is, how old, how sure) and filtered by the reader's role.
parts.seams: The transport; the role filter from the connection registry. One builder per fact serves both the snapshot and the live push.

parts.name: Connections and roles
parts.plain: Every connection presents a verified pass; the engine knows what class it is, its name, which role it has and whether it is still there, by one liveness rule. A client's own word decides nothing.
parts.seams: The kinds of pass (operator, watch-only, device, session) and the ways a connection arrives.

parts.name: Equipment
parts.plain: Each thing the room can do (play a video, play music, play a sound, route and set a volume, light a scene, show a display) behind one interface, with the outside program as an adapter beneath it. The engine's picture of each program is dated and reconciled; one supervisor restarts what it can.
parts.seams: One adapter per program and one software stand-in per capability for the preview engine and the test rig.

parts.name: Show runner
parts.plain: The designer's cues, the game clock, the video queue and the held items: what the room should be doing now, given the game's events and the GM's commands, and what is parked because a service is down or a video is busy. One held store; it reads equipment's dated picture and keeps none of its own.
parts.seams: The cue vocabulary and clock rules from the pack.

parts.name: Verdict
parts.plain: What the game needs against what the kit has tonight, as one calculation whose every line says paper or live and go, no-go or dormant. The editor, the preflight, the start gate and a cue-time refusal all quote it. Already built; what is missing is a route to the screen.
parts.seams: None needed: data in, data out. The caller gathers the live inventory and passes it in.

parts.name: Lifecycle
parts.plain: The table of moments against facts and the only code that moves a game from one moment to the next. Boot and Reset System are the same path; every screen is told the boundary instead of guessing it; it is the only caller of every part's reset.
parts.seams: The host (engine or standalone tablet, the same table). The apply window for a pack change is a row of the table.

parts.name: Venue fit
parts.plain: The venue technician's profile: what the kit brings tonight, which real instrument each of the pack's names binds to, whether the engine starts or adopts each program, how many stations and remote displays to expect; and, if the owner places it here, the declared fact that a game runs with no engine.
parts.seams: The profile file; practice and preview profiles have the same shape.

parts.name: Engine instance
parts.plain: One engine knows its own names (data folder, process files, sockets, ports, the display it drives, the passes it accepts), so a second engine on the same machine, a test, a preview or a second kit, never touches the first. Its parts are built once from one list, by a starting point that sits above them all.
parts.seams: The environment (the settings file, a test's overrides, a preview's). The one list of parts is used by boot, by Reset System and by tests alike.

parts.name: Screens
parts.plain: A screen draws the facts it is delivered, with their labels, and sends requests in the one envelope; it keeps no rule copy and makes no verdict of its own. The GM's four sections, the scoreboard page, the phone's memory view and the hardware scanner's display are each one of these.
parts.seams: One for each kind of device; the scoreboard page is one screen shown in two places, the TV's browser and the Pi 4.

parts.name: Design studio
parts.plain: The designer's drafts, published through the engine's own gate, applied to a running engine at a window the lifecycle allows, rehearsed on a preview engine kept apart from the live one, with verdict badges on the draft. It talks to the engine by message, never by writing its files or borrowing its code.
parts.seams: The draft store; the preview engine as a second engine instance under a preview profile.

parts.name: Joins and proofs
parts.plain: Every shape two parts share is written once and both sides read it; every fake is checked against the class it stands for; the same suite runs on two packs; every level of testing runs the real programs it can, under an engine of its own, so no test reaches a live show.
parts.seams: Shared shapes written once, from the reply words and the facts; a test for each plugged-in program that it does what its part promises; every suite run on two packs.

parts.name: Release
parts.plain: What is installed on a machine is one described set (engine version, built client folders, pack version, media by fingerprint, profile) that the engine compares at start and reports, so a rollback moves everything or says what it did not.
parts.seams: Swapping the blue and green machines as the cutover; one list of what is installed, checked with the verdict's words.

alternatives.title: Getting state onto screens: one part or a delivery per promise
alternatives.a: One delivery part, with one builder per fact for the live change and the catch-up, carrying the label and filtered by role.
alternatives.b: The parts behind each promise deliver their own facts: the game record keeps its broadcasts and snapshot, equipment keeps its own pushes, with only a shared envelope.
alternatives.cost: The candidate needs every part that decides a fact to offer it in one shape, and one store on every screen that holds any fact; it is the only form in which C2, C6 and C10 are removed once. The other way needs less agreement and keeps each promise's delivery local, but C6 and C2 recur per promise and the check that every screen shows each fact's label stays a repeated audit.

alternatives.title: The rules: shared code or two implementations under one contract
alternatives.a: One rules module loaded by the engine and the tablet, with generated tables for the hardware scanner.
alternatives.b: Two bodies of code, one in the engine and one on the tablet, held equal by a test that runs the same inputs through both.
alternatives.cost: The candidate needs the engine's rules packaged so a browser can run them, and a generator for the tables; it removes C9 for the tablet by construction. The other way keeps today's two bodies and relies on a test that runs both and compares them; it detects drift and never removes it.

alternatives.title: Equipment: an interface per capability or per program
alternatives.a: Per capability (play a video, set a volume, light a scene), with the programs, or software stand-ins, plugged in beneath.
alternatives.b: Per program (a supervised process with its own verbs), as today's seven adapters under one supervision rule.
alternatives.cost: The candidate gives the preview engine and the test rig a real second thing to plug in and lets the show runner ask one object whether a video is playing; it costs one interface over programs that work differently (a video queue is not a music playlist). The other way is nearer today's code and cheaper first, but leaves the stand-ins hypothetical and the cross-program questions spread.

alternatives.title: The standalone tablet: the same modules as the engine, or its own engine
alternatives.a: The same game record, lifecycle, answering and delivery hosted on the tablet, with a switch that says the game is standalone.
alternatives.b: A tablet-local engine kept equal by tests, as today but improved.
alternatives.cost: The candidate needs the record, the lifecycle table and answering and delivery to run outside the engine's own runtime, which limits how the engine's code is packaged; it makes parity structural. The other way keeps the engine free of that constraint and keeps a second body of rules on the tablet, with five rules that nothing keeps equal today as the standing risk.

alternatives.title: The tap's answer and the night's record: one part or two
alternatives.a: Two parts: answering at the tap, and the night's record written at the end.
alternatives.b: One part that answers and remembers.
alternatives.cost: Two parts match two people and two moments and give the night's record one input and one reader; they cost a second part with no behaviour today and, if it becomes a promise of its own, a promise no flaw mainly breaks. One part keeps the promise's title whole but puts the record writer beside the reply, which share nothing.

alternatives.title: The lifecycle: a module or a table each part reads
alternatives.a: A lifecycle module, the only mover and the only caller of every reset.
alternatives.b: A table every part reads and applies to its own facts, with no central mover.
alternatives.cost: The candidate removes C5 by construction and breaks today's loop of seven modules; it costs one module that depends on seven others and receives every boundary change, and every part must offer it a reset. The other way keeps each part's reset local and the mover small, but leaves whether every part read the table to a test, the same fault as C5: a list kept by hand that a test must check.

alternatives.title: The scoreboard: one page in two hosts, or a view of the GM app
alternatives.a: One page shown in two places, the TV's browser and the Pi 4.
alternatives.b: The scoreboard as a view inside the GM app, chosen by the pass.
alternatives.cost: The candidate keeps the audience's page apart from the GM's command center and is the smaller change; it keeps two drawings of the same facts, the GM app's and the page's. The other way gives one drawing per fact on every screen and one build, at the cost of a far larger client on a Pi 4 and a pass that must keep the GM's controls off the audience's screen.

alternatives.title: Release day: its own part beside the developer's proof, or in venue fit's deploy chain
alternatives.a: Release as its own small part: the owner's release-day half of proving a change before it reaches anyone.
alternatives.b: Release folded into venue fit's Deploy stage, the venue technician's handoff.
alternatives.cost: Both place C15. The candidate keeps the owner's cutover decision beside the developer's proof; the other way puts the installed-pieces check where the venue technician already works. It is a wording choice.

questionNotes.note: The map favours two parts, answering and the night's record, so either two jobs or one job with its second half filed as the end moment's row in the lifecycle table and a reader in the designer's Review stage. The two halves share no module. The cost of one job is that the GM at the tap and the owner after the show look for their need in one sentence; the cost of two is a new job that no flaw has as its main home.

J8 is one part with an output, venue fit (the installer's profile, bindings, host modes), plus two things that are not parts: the authority switch, a setting every rule takes, and the naming layer, which J10 owns and J6 and J8 share. That favours a rename over a split, since a new eleventh job would have no part of its own. Two renames fit: 'Fit the game to the venue, whatever the setup', which keeps the standalone GM and other kits in the title, and 'Fit the game to the venue it is in tonight', which leaves them to a clause and a rule.

The map splits J10 by moment: the developer's green run is a quality carried by the proofs and the engine instance over every part; release day is one small part with one person and one moment, touching only the pack channel, the instance's names and the verdict's words. Widening the sentence, splitting it, or filing release day in J8's deploy chain all place C15; C16 lands on the proofs whichever way. Leaving J10 as drafted also fits the parts; its cost is that release day stays unnamed in a sentence about tests.

Neither sentence needs to carry the route. The route is one delivery part used by J2, J4, J9, J1, J7 and J5. Equipment decides its state and health as one dated object; delivery carries it; screens draw it with its label. If one job must hold the words, both fit: in J4, the words sit with the equipment, but J4 then names a route J2 also needs; in J2, they match the vocabulary, which files the video queue, music, held items, the clock and each service's health inside runtime state, but J2 then carries equipment beside the game's record.

Both of J1's added clauses land on parts. Nothing in the engine assumes ALN is the generic quality carried by the rules (only from the pack) and by venue fit and the engine instance (kit names only from the profile and the instance). Every part runs the same version and says which is the pack channel's stamp on every copy and every game record, compared when a connection is admitted. Each clause has a part to stand on, which supports keeping both; the owner confirms.
Connections and roles holds both halves, the pass and the grants, and answering checks the floor once from it. The widened J7 matches one part.

The map supports the clause: a declared standalone game is a setting every rule takes, and J8, the job that fits the game to tonight's setup, is where it is declared. Where the fact is held is a later choice; the installer's profile is the candidate the map favours, because the dormancy idea (a profile with no engine equipment, so every engine duty reads dormant) already carries the right words. The pack, the game record or each device are the alternatives; whichever is chosen, the pack channel carries the declaration to every device.
